content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors propose an approach for early stop training. Their approach is based on variance of activations of convolutional layers: training is stopped if the variance remains steady enough. The approach could save computational costs of training if its limited.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- There are several numerical results that demonstrates effectiveness. It seems to somehow work in most of cases (even though it looks like there is accuracy drop in some cases)

Major weaknesses:
- The method seems quite adhoc. For example, the rounding in feels quite arbitrary choice. Same conclusion could be reached without rounding just checking if difference is less than a threshold. They do not give any theoretical background related to their choices. E.g. that why variance should be inspected or why rounding? I feel that similar results could be reached by observing when the validation metric gets steady enough. 

- Numerical results: I think validation iteration should not be included in CTS metric. The baseline runs are trained with a pre-defined number of epochs, i.e., the validation iteration included in the metrics are not used in the baseline approach. Also, in practice, you do not need to run validation iteration each epoch if you want to save in computational complexity. Including the validation iteration in CTS just gives impression that savings are bigger than in practice. 

- The story is somewhat misleading: the abstract talks about observing generalisation gap as a stopping criterion to avoid overfitting. This gives impression that the paper will talk about early stopping in overfitting related topics. However, numerical experiments do not seem to include any case in which overfitting would be present. 

- Related to above, I have some doubts that their method actually would work in a case in which overfitting is present. Would the variance based metric stay steady when model starts to overfit?  

Minor weakness:
- The plots are too small. The font size is too small to read without a magnifying lens or zooming in PDF.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
In general, the method is described well. The approach is described with a good clarity and easy to understand. Results should be reproducible if one wants. Their approach seems novel, or at least I have not 

However, the story is bit misleading as mentioned above.
content.summary_of_the_review: As contribution is quite thin and there are some major issues, I would recommend rejection, or at least major revision if possible.

content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed to monitor standard deviations of CNN outputs to identify convergence from training data only, without the use of validation data. An empirical evaluation is conducted on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and SVHN, where the proposed method saves 68.35% training time as compared to the validation based baseline.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well-written and easy to follow. Related work is described throughly. Experimental results confirm the paper hypothesis, and demonstrate a high training time savings cost. 

However, one of the key uses of the validation dataset is to test on unseen data. By evaluating on data seen during training, model generalization is no longer being evaluated. This issue can cause significant overfitting and biased behaviors, and raises an ethical concern. While the authors mention generalization in Section 4.4, no generalization analysis of whether the models trained with the proposed method overfit to the training distribution is conducted. In addition, experiments in Section 4.4 could be clarified and expanded upon. Finally, it would be interesting whether stability based training affects evaluation metrics (e.g., TP, FP etc.) in the same was as it does with accuracy.

As a possible alternative to address the above concern, have the authors tried monitoring stability vectors on the validation dataset during periodic evaluations?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and demonstrates a significant (68.35%) improvement in training time by monitoring standard deviations of neural network outputs. However, relying only on the training set takes away the possibility to accurately detect overfitting, a crucial concern in modern AI applications. Only a limited discussion and evaluation of this issue is provided, while this is a central issue.
content.summary_of_the_review: Well-written paper with strong empirical results, but takes away evaluation of overfitting, and as as result, could raise ethical issues.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a hypothesis for anticipating the near-optimal learning capacity of a CNN by analyzing the data variation across all the convolutional layers of the network. The authors introduced a stability vector computed for each layer. No validation data is required for this approach and can be used with any CNN variant without requiring any additional trainable parameters. The authors analysed the change in variance of each layer at every epoch in comparison to the previous epoch. If the difference between mean of variance for each layer between epoch e and e-1 becomes zero and it happens for two more epochs consistently then the features have been learnt and have become stable, then the training should be stopped and now this model can be used testing on validation and test data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
A nice concept of using data variation while estimating the near-optimal learning capacity of the network
No additional parameters required
Hypothesis introduced in the paper saves total computation time during the training period.

Queries:
Do all the layers stabilize at the same time/ at the same epoch?
For how many layers the stability value should be zero to stop training?
Will it work for deeper CNN’s with a huge number of layers? Does it have a memory constraint to store the stability vectors like if we use imagenet as it has 1 million samples then if we store 1million/batch size number of samples: it would take lot of storage space?
What happens if instead of rounding off and if difference of mean of variances at epoch e and e-1 is 0 then stops, rather if we don’t do round off and use thresholding (tending to 0) to stop when difference between mean of variances less than equal to threshold?
As per the figure1 stability of each layer is being checked before non-linearity layer, why not calculating stability after non-linearty layer? Also, if we use a batch-norm layer can we use those standard-deviations calculated for checking the stability.
Please show comparison with early-stopping technique of deciding when to stop after checking the gap between training and validation loss curves.
This strategy seems to may work for Neural networks having FC’s also why not this work for those kind of neural networks and as per suggested in paper it will work for CNN’s only.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3532 by Reviewer GJDn

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper suggest to replace early stopping based on the performances over a validation set by a measure of the standard deviations of the intermediate layers outputs of convolutional neural networks across different iterations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:

- **Misunderstanding of the concept of early stopping** The authors don't understand the concept of early stopping. They wrote "it monitors the average loss function on the validation set and continues training until it falls below the value of the training set objective, at which the training procedure is halted". It's just false. If we look at what is wrote in Goodfellow et al 2017, it's just "The algorithm terminates when no parameters have improved over the best recorded validation error for some pre-speciﬁed number of iterations ". There is nothing about the validation curve falling below the training curve or not ! It's just about does your validation error improve or not. Furthermore, they wrote that "the objective on the validation set might ever not reach its target value". What do you mean by target value of the validation set ? Is it zero ? What about the potential noise in the data ? The only thing that is not guarantee is that if you have enough data, your validation error might never go up (which is a good thing). The whole justification about why one shouldn't use early stopping doesn't make any sense. Same in the conclusion, the authors wrote "for early stopping, validation error with train loss is used to identify the generalization gap", it doesn't make sense because early stopping depend only on the validation error (you don't need the training loss for anything there). This misunderstanding is also showed in the abstract "Current practice is to stop training when loss decreases and the gap between training and validation error increases". No ones does that ! If you do, you will probably end up the training after 2 iterations ! Maybe in the first iterations your training error will decrease much more than your validation error (like the model is picking on easy features which don't generalize on the validation set) but after a while the model learn to pick other features that will generalize better, thus reducing the gap we had in the beginning. The only formulation of early stopping that is valid is simply to save the model that has the best validation error and if the validation error doesn't improve after a given number of epochs, then stop training. 

- **The proposed method doesn't make sense** The authors suggest to compute the variance of the intermediate output representations across different training step. But the variance of the intermediate representation is a function of the parameters of the neural network and the magnitude of the change in the parameters across different training setup depend of the learning rate ! The authors never discuss how the learning rate might play a role in their metric.  Furthermore, many convolutional networks presented in this paper use batch normalization which play an important role in the scale of the activation. You can't write a paper about measuring the variance in the output representation without taking into consideration the role of the learning rate or batch normalization.

- **The experimental setup does not correspond to the claim made by the paper**. The author suggest a method to replace early stopping (with a validation set) but never used early stopping as their baseline. Furthermore, they made experiment with CBS but never explain how CBS is relevant in this paper ?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper does lack clarity, quality and novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is built upon a profond misunderstanding of the concept of early stopping. In consequence, there are important issues with the entire paper. The authors suggest to use an early stopping based on the measure of the variances of intermediate representation across training iterations but never take into consideration the impact of the learning rate. Furthermore using the variance of the output of different layer of a CCN is probably not a good direction because when using learning rate scheduling or adaptive learning you will by construction reduce the magnitude of the change in the parameters space, thus in the activations.

content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to monitor the standard deviations of output from each layer as a way to decide when to stop training the network. Authors demonstrate that in regular image classification task (with relatively simple datasets), and 6 CNN architectures, this provides about ~58% time savings when compared to relying on a fixed number of epochs for training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Is the problem in the paper well justified? There authors are not working with an extremely small dateset that a validation set cannot be separated out. In my personal opinion, the motivation for the problem itself is unclear. 

Problems with the method:
1. Why do the authors expect the method would provide good generalization as opposed to just "overfitting"? Behavior of stopping would depend on the hyper parameter r which was fixed as 2 in the paper without any justification or experiments. Likely selecting a good r for "generalization" would need a validation set, underscoring the purpose of the paper. 
2. There'll be complex interaction of learning rate scheduling with this method that the paper completely overlooks and does not discuss. 

Insufficient experiments:
The paper lacks very basic baselines: (a) stop when training loss doesn't change much (I suspect this will achieve almost the same result to the proposed method in the paper), (b) compare to stopping with a validation set (this should. be done at least to demonstrate competitive advantage of the paper)!
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clear writing, but experiments are low quality, and the contributions are not novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem is not well motivated, the proposed method is not well justified, and empirical experiments are not thorough and baselines are inadequate. I recommend a clear rejection in the current state.
